title: My soul thirsteth (Psalm 62 [63])
hook: the Sunday morning psalm: early I seek thee in a dry land

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Miserere, David's psalm after his great sin. Your line was a clean heart. Today, a morning psalm.

What's the first thing you reach for in the morning? For most people it's the phone, before the eyes are fully open: messages, news, the weather, somebody's vacation photos. The first minute of the day goes to whatever is loudest. An old Christian habit gives that minute to something else. For centuries, monks and nuns greeted the first light with one particular psalm, a song that starts with a person awake early, thirsty, in a dry place.
screen: `THE FIRST THING YOU REACH FOR.` → `THE FIRST MINUTE OF THE DAY.` → `A PSALM BEFORE DAWN.`

segments.voice: Psalm 62 in the Douay, 63 in most Bibles. Its heading places David in the desert, far from the sanctuary. The Douay begins: "O God, my God, to thee do I watch at break of day." The Hebrew verb comes from the word for dawn: I seek you at first light. That's why many English Bibles say early will I seek thee. Then the thirst: my soul thirsts for you, my flesh longs for you, like a dry, weary land where there is no water. Not just the soul; the body too. Then a line that stops people: "For thy mercy is better than lives." Lives, plural. Better than life itself, better than any number of lives. Then the night. If I have remembered you on my bed, the psalm says, I will think of you in the morning. The one praying has been awake in the dark, and wakes still turned toward God. It ends with closeness so physical it's almost a hug: "My soul hath stuck close to thee: thy right hand hath received me." Clinging, the way a child holds a parent's leg. Saint John Chrysostom, in the fourth century, said the fathers before him had appointed it to be sung every morning. Today in the Liturgy of the Hours it opens Morning Prayer on Sundays and on great feasts. The first minute of the day, given to thirst.
screen: `TO THEE DO I WATCH AT BREAK OF DAY.` · `A DRY LAND WITH NO WATER.` · `THY MERCY IS BETTER THAN LIVES.` · `MY SOUL HATH STUCK CLOSE TO THEE.`

segments.voice: Picture the moment you wake, eyes still heavy, the phone somewhere nearby, and before you touch it, one line: O God, my God, to thee do I watch at break of day. Say it now, three times, slowly, so it's ready for the morning. If you pray, let it be your first word to God tomorrow; if you don't, let it be a way of choosing what gets your first minute.
Shachar. Hebrew for dawn, the root of the morning psalm's seek you early, a person awake at first light, thirsty for God in a dry land. Today's word.
Your line: early I seek you. Before the loudest thing gets there. That's day one hundred seventy-two.

what a scholar hears: the Hebrew verb is built on shachar, dawn; and where the Hebrew heading says the wilderness of Judah, the Latin and the Douay say Edom.

notes: Douay Psalm 62 wording (verses 2, 4, 9): confirm against a Challoner edition.
Hebrew ashachareka from shachar (dawn); the KJV 'early will I seek thee' is mentioned as 'many English Bibles', not quoted. Confirm the Hebrew form and pronunciation.
Heading: Hebrew 'in the wilderness of Judah'; Vulgate 'in deserto Idumaeae' (Douay 'Edom'). Confirm.
Chrysostom on Psalm 140: the fathers ordained Psalm 62 for morning and 140 for evening. Paraphrased; confirm reference.
Liturgy of the Hours: Psalm 63 at Morning Prayer, Sunday of Week I, and on solemnities and feasts. Confirm.
Carry 'early I seek you' matches the KJV/Hebrew sense rather than the Douay's 'watch at break of day'; the teach explains the link.

Audit (second sample): the hook no longer says monks 'began the day' with this psalm (Matins/Vigils came first; Psalm 62 belonged to Lauds at daybreak); the heading is no longer said to mention 'no water' (that is verse 2's image, not the title); Chrysostom's remark is now attributed to 'the fathers', as he puts it, not 'the early Christians'.
